Therapeutic and mechanistic evaluation of Piperlongumine in oral squamous cell carcinoma: An integrated in vitro and in silico approach

Abstract:

Abstract

Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) comprises about 90% of oral cancer. To withstand the side effects of chemotherapy, phytotherapy is widely used as an alternative to chemotherapy. Research on phytocompounds has uncovered promising new insights for treating various cancers, including oral cancer, offering a clear advantage over conventional chemotherapy by overcoming chemoresistance with negligible side effects. Piperlongumine (PIP) is a biologically active alkaloid found primarily in the fruits and roots of the Piper longum plant. PIP exhibits potent cytotoxic, anti-proliferative, and apoptotic properties in many cancers. However, the anti-cancer potential of PIP in oral cancer is still unraveled. The cytotoxic potential of PIP in the oral cancer cell line SCC9 and H357 were investigated using the MTT assay, which showed an IC50 of 4.7 and 3.5 &muM respectively, while the normal HaCaT cells showed comparatively lower sensitivity (IC50 16.6 &muM). The anti-colonizing and anti-migratory potential of PIP in SCC9 and H357 cells were observed in a dose and time dependent manner through colony and scratch assay respectively. Increased intracellular ROS and mitochondrial superoxide, accompanied by reduced mitochondrial membrane potential and mitochondrial mass, were observed following PIP treatment NAC and MitoTEMPO attenuated the corresponding oxidative responses. AO/EtBr and DAPI staining demonstrated concentration-dependent apoptotic responses, while comet assay and &gamma-H2AX immunofluorescence confirmed DNA damage. The anticancer activity of PIP was further supported in an ex vivo tumoroid model, where PIP reduced spheroid size and increased apoptotic cells. Although our studies have demonstrated the anti-cancer effects of PIP, the network-level molecular mechanisms underlying its activity in OSCC remain poorly understood. To bridge this gap, we employed a comprehensive integrative computational framework to identify key hub genes associated with OSCC progression. Differentially expressed transcriptomic datasets were identified from publicly available databases. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks constructed using STRING and analyzed with Cytoscape, cytoHubba, and MCODE identified the top hub genes, including BIRC5, CDK1, BUB1, MAD2L1, and KIF23. Molecular docking showed potent binding of PIP to the hub genes, most notably CDK1 (-7.8 kcal/mol), driven by hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions. However, 100 ns molecular dynamics, MM/PBSA, and free-energy landscape analyses supported greater structural and energetic stability of the BIRC5-PIP complex over CDK1-PIP, demonstrating the importance of molecular dynamic analyses for target prioritization.&nbsp SwissADME ensures good pharmacokinetics of PIP. The above in silico findings were confirmed by qRT-PCR and cell cycle analysis. Through this multi-omics network approach combined with experimental validation, the present study offers valuable mechanistic insights and identifies PIP as a promising candidate for therapeutic development.
